mcq.q: The model proposes refund(order_id, amount). What decides the amount?
options: Deterministic code from the order record and policy
mcq.why: The model proposes; code computes amounts and enforces limits.

mcq.q: Where should a tenant ID for a tool call come from?
mcq.why: Identity and tenant come from trusted context, never from model output.

mcq.q: What is the core pattern for combining a model with business rules?
options: The model interprets and proposes; deterministic code validates, decides and executes
Rules are written into the prompt
mcq.why: Rules must be exact, auditable and identical every time.
distractors: Model output is a suggestion from a distribution.

mcq.q: Which jobs suit the model?
options: Understanding intent, extracting fields, drafting wording, ranking options
mcq.why: Fuzzy tasks go to the model; exact ones to code.
distractors: Permissions must be enforced in code.

mcq.q: Which jobs belong in code?
options: Amounts, limits, permissions, state transitions and legal text
mcq.why: These must be exact and auditable.

mcq.q: A prompt says “apply a 10% discount for customers over 2 years, max $500”. In production some customers get 15%. What is the fix?
options: Move the rule into code; the model only extracts that the customer requests a discount
mcq.why: Exact, testable and auditable behaviour needs code.
distractors: Instructions do not make rules exact.

mcq.q: The model replies “done” but the database write failed. What should the system report?
options: The actual result of the write
Success, to keep the user happy
mcq.why: Never report success from model text.
distractors: The model does not know whether the write succeeded.

mcq.q: What should the boundary between model and rules look like?
options: Free text passed to the database
A typed proposal that code accepts, modifies or rejects, with the reason logged
mcq.why: Explicit boundaries make behaviour auditable.
distractors: Free text is not safe to act on.

mcq.q: The model extracts “2 seats” when the account has 5. What catches it?
mcq.why: Check extracted values against systems of record.

mcq.q: Which tool guarantees that a local model's output matches a JSON Schema or grammar by masking tokens?
mcq.why: Instructor, by contrast, validates and re-asks on failure.
distractors: LiteLLM is a unified API and gateway.
DSPy optimises prompts against a metric.

interview.q: Explain the “model proposes, code disposes” pattern.
Which parts of a refund flow belong to the model and which to code?
Why are prompted business rules unreliable?
covers: No audit trail of the rule

interview.q: A team wants the model to decide discounts from the chat. How do you redesign it?
covers: Rule in code with clear inputs
interview.followUp: How would you show the business owner the rule now behaves exactly as written?

interview.q: How do you make sure users see the true outcome of an action?
covers: Read the result from the system
Never trust model claims of success

interview.q: {company}'s assistant explains fee waivers. Design how waivers are actually decided and recorded.
Design the boundary between an LLM and a workflow engine for an enterprise assistant.
{assistant} changes bookings. Design the flow so fees, rules and outcomes are always exact.
covers: Code applies fare rules and computes fees
Supplier call result decides the outcome

mcq.q: Which errors are worth retrying?
mcq.why: Rate limits and transient server errors can succeed later; a 400 is your bug.

mcq.q: Which timeouts should an LLM call have?
options: Only a timeout on the response body size
A connect timeout, a total deadline and, for streaming, an idle timeout between tokens
mcq.why: LLM latency has a long tail; without deadlines, connections pile up.

mcq.q: Backoff waits base × 2^attempt. With a base of 0.5 s, how long is the wait before attempt 3 (counting from 0)?
mcq.why: 0.5 × 2³ = 4 s, then randomised by jitter.
distractors: That uses a base of 1 s.

mcq.q: Why add jitter to retries?
options: To reduce the number of attempts
To spread retries out so clients do not retry in synchronised spikes
mcq.why: Synchronised retries can knock a recovering service over again.

mcq.q: A provider returns 429 with a Retry-After header. What should the client do?
options: Wait at least the time it asks for
mcq.why: Respect the server's guidance.

mcq.q: What is a client-side token bucket for?
options: Tracking request and token rate limits so you queue rather than get rejected
mcq.why: Providers limit requests and tokens per minute.

mcq.q: Why must fallback models be evaluated too?
options: Their output quality and format may differ
mcq.why: A fallback that breaks the format causes new failures.

mcq.q: Which are token budgets the topic recommends? Choose all that apply.
mcq.why: Budgets bound cost and latency.
distractors: Unbounded output is a cost and latency risk.

mcq.q: Retrying without a retry budget or admission control during a slowdown tends to…
options: Turn the slowdown into an outage
mcq.why: Retries add load exactly when capacity is short.

mcq.q: 20% of 2,000 requests per second fail, and each failure is retried up to 3 times. How much extra load can that add?
mcq.why: 400 failures × 3 retries = 1,200 more requests per second at worst.

interview.q: Which errors are worth retrying, and how?
What timeouts does an LLM call need?
Why do retries need jitter?
Design a call wrapper for LLM requests.
interview.followUp: What would you log on every retry?

interview.q: Your provider is rate-limiting you at peak. What do you do?
{company}'s refund call timed out. Should you retry, and how?
covers: Never blindly: it may have succeeded
Query status with an idempotency key

interview.q: Design resilience for an assistant during a provider outage.
{company}'s festival sale starts with provider throttling. Design the client behaviour so retries do not make it worse.

mcq.q: How does the cost shape of a hosted API differ from self-hosting?
options: Hosted is per token and scales to zero; self-hosted is per GPU-hour and cheap only at high, steady utilisation
mcq.why: Idle GPUs still cost money; hosted APIs charge only for use (14.8).
distractors: At very high steady volume self-hosting can win.
At low or spiky volume it usually loses.

mcq.q: Which option gives full control over data, including air-gapped operation?
mcq.why: Hosted data control depends on contract, region and retention settings.

mcq.q: Why are public leaderboards a weak basis for choosing a model?
options: They measure general skills on public data, which may be contaminated and rarely matches your task
mcq.why: Build a task-specific evaluation set instead.
distractors: They are informative, just not about your task.

mcq.q: How large should a first task-specific evaluation set be, according to the topic?
options: About 50–200 real examples with expected outcomes
mcq.why: Small enough to build quickly, large enough to compare 3–5 candidates.
distractors: Far more than needed to start.

mcq.q: Model A scores 92% at $0.01 per request; model B 88% at $0.002. The acceptance bar is 85%. Which should you choose?
mcq.why: Choose the cheapest model that meets the bar; B passes at a fifth of the cost.
distractors: A is better but costs five times more than needed.

mcq.q: What should a model comparison measure together?
mcq.why: A model that is accurate but too slow or expensive fails the product.
distractors: An advertised length is not evidence.

mcq.q: 150 tickets are labelled by two people, and the 140 they agree on are kept with a short scoring script. What does this become?
options: Your baseline, model-selection tool and first regression test
mcq.why: Chapter 8 grows it into a full evaluation practice.
distractors: Far too small and the wrong purpose.

mcq.q: Which is an operational risk specific to hosted APIs?
options: GPU failures in your data centre
Provider outages, rate limits and model deprecations
mcq.why: Self-hosting swaps these for your own on-call and capacity work.

mcq.q: A team picks a model because it advertises a 1M-token context. What is wrong?
options: An advertised capability is not task evidence; measure on your own cases
Long contexts are always used well
mcq.why: Choose with your own data (5.3, 5.7).

mcq.q: When should you re-run your model comparison?
mcq.why: New releases and price changes can change the cheapest model that meets the bar (18.5).

interview.q: Compare hosted APIs with self-hosted open models.
Why should you not choose a model from a public leaderboard?
What does “choose the cheapest model that meets the bar” mean in practice?
Build a first evaluation set for a ticket-classification feature. Walk through it.
covers: Script for accuracy per category, latency, cost
Use as baseline and regression test
interview.followUp: How would you keep the set representative as traffic changes?

interview.q: Your company must keep customer data in-country. How does that change model selection?
covers: Contract and region terms for hosted options

interview.q: {company} must choose a model for shopper questions in four languages at festival-peak volume. How would you decide?
covers: A routing mix: mid-size default, frontier for escalation

interview.q: Design a model-selection process the company repeats every quarter.
{company} is choosing models for its booking agent. How would you assign models to steps?

mcq.q: Which message roles does a typical chat API use?
mcq.why: System holds the developer's persistent instructions; tool holds results of tool calls.

mcq.q: Why put the stable parts of a prompt first?
options: They can be prompt-cached, and variable parts go last
Models ignore the end of prompts
mcq.why: A stable prefix can be reused across requests (14.3).

mcq.q: Why delimit retrieved context clearly, for example with XML-style tags?
options: Because models cannot read plain text
So the model can tell data from instructions, which also matters for security
mcq.why: It helps against instructions hidden in documents (16.2).

mcq.q: How many few-shot examples does the topic suggest, and what kind?
options: 2–5 diverse input→output pairs showing format and edge cases
mcq.why: Examples are strong signals; diversity stops the model copying surface details.
distractors: Examples help format and edge cases.

mcq.q: All your few-shot examples use the same customer name and product. What risk does this create?
options: The model copies those surface details into unrelated answers
mcq.why: Vary the examples' surface features.

mcq.q: How should instructions be written?
options: Specific and positive, with the reason when it helps the model generalise
mcq.why: For example: “answer in under 80 words”.
distractors: Positive instructions work better than lists of don'ts.

mcq.q: What does prompt versioning involve?
options: Saving prompts in a chat history
An ID and version, review, evaluation on every change, and the version logged with each request
mcq.why: Treat prompts as code (18.1).

mcq.q: A team keeps adding instructions without re-running the regression suite. What tends to happen?
options: New rules conflict with old ones, and regressions go unnoticed
mcq.why: Every change needs the evaluation set.

mcq.q: Where should the user's input go in a well-structured prompt?
mcq.why: Role, instructions, context, examples and format come before it.

mcq.q: A customer complains about one specific answer. What lets you trace exactly which instructions produced it?
options: The prompt version logged with that request
The current prompt in the repository
mcq.why: The current prompt may have changed since then.
distractors: The model alone does not identify the prompt.
It may differ from what was used.

interview.q: Describe the anatomy of a well-structured prompt.
When do few-shot examples help, and how can they hurt?
Why treat prompts as code?
A prompt change improved one case and broke three others. How should the process have caught it?
interview.followUp: How would you decide whether to ship a change that helps one slice and hurts another?

interview.q: How do you structure a prompt so retrieved documents cannot act as instructions?
covers: State that they are not instructions
Never rely on the prompt alone (16.2)

interview.q: {company}'s compliance team must approve every change to customer-facing prompts. Design the workflow.
covers: Prompts in the repository with IDs

interview.q: Design a prompt registry for a team running 30 prompts in production.
How would you write an extraction prompt for {company}'s multilingual booking requests, and test it?
covers: Diverse examples across languages and trip types

mcq.q: What is context engineering?
options: Deciding, for every call, exactly which tokens go into the window
mcq.why: The window is a budget shared by instructions, tools, history, documents and output.

mcq.q: What happens when you include too much context?
options: Calls get slower and costlier, and the model is distracted by irrelevant material
mcq.why: Too little and it guesses; too much and quality and cost suffer.
distractors: It is processed and can distract.

mcq.q: How do context assemblers usually prioritise?
options: Instructions and the current question first, then by relevance; drop the lowest first
mcq.why: Greedy inclusion by priority within the budget.
distractors: Recency is one factor at most.

mcq.q: Which are compression techniques mentioned in the topic? Choose all that apply.
mcq.why: Replacing long tool outputs with extracted key fields is another.
distractors: The system prompt is always included.

mcq.q: Where should the most important material go in a long context?
options: Near the start or the end
mcq.why: Models attend less reliably to the middle of very long contexts.
distractors: The middle is the least reliable place.

mcq.q: A recipe has system 900, tools 600, account facts 200, chunks 2,500, summary 300, last turns 800 tokens and an output reserve of 800. What is the total?
mcq.why: 5,300 tokens of input plus the 800-token output reserve.

mcq.q: That 6,100-token recipe runs in a 16,000-token window. Roughly what share of the window does it use?
mcq.why: 6,100 ÷ 16,000 ≈ 38%, which is faster and cheaper than filling the window.
distractors: It leaves most of the window free.

mcq.q: Compression shortened a policy clause and the answer became wrong. What was likely lost?
options: An exception clause or effective date the answer depended on
mcq.why: Mark decision-critical text as never-summarise.

mcq.q: Why must the budget include the output reserve?
options: Output tokens share the same context window
mcq.why: Otherwise a long answer is cut off.
distractors: Output costs tokens and window space.
It is for the model's answer.
It is a design rule, not a provider rule.

mcq.q: In the assembler, you shrink the budget. What is dropped first?
mcq.why: Always-included items stay; lower-priority ones go or get compressed.

interview.q: What is context engineering, and why does it matter?
covers: The model knows only its context
A budget shared by many sources
Too little: guessing; too much: cost and distraction

interview.q: Describe the steps of assembling context for a call.
Why does placement inside the context matter?
covers: Middle of long contexts used less reliably
Important items near start or end

interview.q: Write a context recipe for a support assistant and justify each part.
covers: Reranked chunks, dropped from the bottom
interview.followUp: What would you cut first if latency doubled?

interview.q: How would you detect that context compression is losing critical details?
covers: Test cases that depend on exceptions and dates
Compare answers with and without compression

interview.q: Design {company}'s context for a dispute summary, and say what must never be summarised.
covers: Policy clauses with effective dates verbatim

interview.q: Design a context-assembly service shared by several assistants.
How would you measure whether a context recipe is good?
covers: Task success on an evaluation set

mcq.q: What is structured output?
options: The model returns data in a declared format, usually JSON matching a JSON Schema
mcq.why: It makes model output usable by code.
distractors: Streaming is about delivery, not format.
Tool results come from your code.

mcq.q: What does constrained decoding guarantee?
options: The output parses against the schema
mcq.why: It masks tokens that would break the schema; it guarantees shape, not truth.
distractors: Valid JSON can contain a wrong amount.

mcq.q: The model returns valid JSON with the wrong refund amount. What was missing?
options: Semantic checks in code against the source data
mcq.why: Validate values, not only shape.

mcq.q: In tool calling, what does the model actually do?
options: It asks for a call with arguments; your code decides whether to execute it
mcq.why: The model proposes; deterministic code disposes.

mcq.q: The model requests get_order(id="A-1043"). Who checks that this user may access that order?
options: Your application code, using the authenticated session
mcq.why: Never trust model-supplied IDs for authorisation (16.3).
distractors: IDs can belong to someone else.

mcq.q: What does streaming improve?
options: Perceived latency: users see the first words sooner
mcq.why: Both versions finish at the same time.

mcq.q: You stream JSON to the UI. When should your code act on it?
options: Only after validating the complete object
As soon as the first field arrives
mcq.why: Partial JSON may be incomplete or invalid.

mcq.q: How should large tool results be returned to the model?
mcq.why: Large results waste context and can distract.
distractors: Tool results go in tool messages.
The model needs the result to answer.

mcq.q: Small local models make more tool-call mistakes. Why is that useful in a lab?
options: You see the failure modes your validation must handle
It proves big models are perfect
mcq.why: Wrong arguments and unnecessary calls are what validation is for.

mcq.q: A create_ticket tool needs a customer ID. Where should it come from?
mcq.why: The model may supply someone else's ID.

interview.q: Explain structured outputs and constrained decoding.
Walk through the tool-calling handshake.
What does streaming improve, and what does it complicate?
covers: Act only on complete validated objects

interview.q: A model proposes a valid tool call that would access another customer's data. Where should that be stopped?
covers: Authorisation in code, not the model
interview.followUp: How would you test this regularly?

interview.q: How would you validate extracted amounts and dates beyond schema checks?
{assistant} calls search, hold and confirm tools. Design the validation at each step.
covers: Schema and request match before search
Hold only options from the search result
Confirm only after the traveller agrees
Check supplier responses, not model claims

interview.q: Design a tool-calling layer shared by several assistants.
covers: Tool registry with schemas and owners

interview.q: {company} extracts dispute fields with an LLM. Design the checks so a wrong amount can never reach a refund.

mcq.q: Why must an application resend conversation history?
options: Model APIs are stateless: each call must include everything the model should know
mcq.why: “Memory” is something your application builds.

mcq.q: What is the weakness of a sliding window over recent turns?
options: It forgets facts stated early, such as an account ID
mcq.why: Simple, but early facts fall out.

mcq.q: What does “summarise and window” keep?
options: A running summary of older turns plus recent turns verbatim
mcq.why: Summaries keep the gist but can drop exact values.

mcq.q: What does fact extraction add?
options: Durable facts in a structured store, injected as needed
mcq.why: Structured values cannot be lost in a later summary.

mcq.q: What must persistent memory across sessions include?
mcq.why: Remembered facts are personal data (11.4, 16.5).
distractors: Users should see what is remembered.

mcq.q: What is the system of record for a conversation?
options: The full transcript in your own database
mcq.why: The context is a working view.
distractors: You need your own records for audit.

mcq.q: A user says at turn 3 they are on an EU data-residency plan and asks at turn 40 about a US-only feature. A pure sliding window answers “yes”. What fixes it?
options: Extract the plan as a fact and let a rule block the feature
Asking the user again every turn
mcq.why: Structured facts plus a deterministic rule (7.7).
distractors: Length does not restore the fact.

mcq.q: A 24-turn conversation averages 200 tokens per turn. Keeping only the last 6 turns uses how many tokens instead of the full history?
A client sends a conversation ID. Can your service treat it as proof the user may read that conversation?
options: No: check that the authenticated user owns it
mcq.why: IDs are identifiers, not authorisation.
distractors: IDs leak and can be guessed.

mcq.q: What do summaries tend to lose?
options: Exact values such as IDs, amounts and dates
mcq.why: Use fact extraction for values that must survive.

interview.q: Why are model APIs stateless, and what does that mean for chat products?
covers: Memory is built by the application

interview.q: Compare sliding windows, summaries and fact extraction.
What is the system of record for a conversation, and why?
A user complains the assistant forgot their account ID halfway through a chat. How do you fix the design?
interview.followUp: How would you test that the fix holds for 100-turn conversations?

interview.q: What controls should persistent memory across sessions have?
{assistant} booked for one traveller when the chat had said four. Design the memory so this cannot happen.
covers: Every booking step reads the record

interview.q: Design conversation storage and compaction for an assistant with millions of users.
covers: Transcript store with IDs and timestamps

interview.q: How would you evaluate whether a compaction strategy loses task-critical details?
covers: Scripted long conversations with planted facts
